source.title_on_document: Interactions with generative AI chatbots: unveiling dialogic dynamics, students' perceptions, and practical competencies in creative problem-solving

supplement.where: No separate supplementary material or online appendix is identified in the document. The article's printed Appendix is included on PDF pp. 25-26: Table 8 (questionnaire), Table 9 (interview outline), and Table 10 (proposal-scoring rubric). Data are available upon reasonable request (p. 27).
supplement.holds: The included article appendix contains instruments and rubric descriptors. No separate supplement is identified as holding outcome standard errors, pretest descriptive statistics, adjusted means, dimension scores, or participant-flow information.

paper_design_summary: Eighty first-semester PhD students at one Chinese university were randomly assigned, 40 per arm, to develop a research proposal through five weekly half-hour dialogues with the generative AI chatbot Dou Bao or with a self-chosen peer (pp. 7-9). Two independent markers scored the submitted proposals with a rubric including originality and a stated maximum of 100; ANCOVA used the prior PhD-application proposal score as covariate (pp. 9-13, 26). Table 7 reports 40 people per arm but contains inconsistent ANCOVA statistics, so the exact analyzed sample is unresolved; AI availability during final writing and the markers' qualifications are not stated (pp. 8-10, 12, 20).

studies.label: Chatbot vs peer dialogue for developing a PhD research proposal

assignment.what_was_assigned: Dialogue partner for developing a research proposal over five weekly sessions: the generative AI chatbot Dou Bao (experimental group) or one self-chosen peer (control group).
assignment.quote: Then they were randomly assigned to either the experimental or the control group, each comprising 40 students.

arms.name: Experimental group (student-GAI chatbot interaction)
arms.description: After a 3-hour training session, five weekly 30-minute individual dialogue sessions with Dou Bao, by text or speech, on five themes (research topic, research questions, literature, research design, originality); then submitted a new research proposal.

arms.name: Control group (student-peer interaction)
arms.description: The same training, five weekly 30-minute sessions, themes, and goal, held with one peer each student chose; no access to similar AI tools during the study period; then submitted a new research proposal.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or withdrawals are enumerated for the proposal outcome. Table 7 reports N = 40 per arm (p. 20), but its F, numerator df, and partial eta-squared are inconsistent with that analyzed total under the ANCOVA model described on p. 13; the exact total and arm-specific analysis counts are therefore null. The printed counts are retained in the outcome's reported statistics. The perception survey analyzed N = 36 per arm (Table 6, p. 19), fewer than the 40 randomized per arm (p. 8); the reason is not stated, and these survey counts do not establish the proposal ANCOVA sample. See final.challenge_resolution for the conditional consistency calculation.
participants.who: First-semester PhD students in education specialisms (international education, student development, educational leadership and management, curriculum development and pedagogy); 32 male and 48 female, aged 26 to 31; volunteers; none had used GAI chatbots for CPS tasks before the study.
participants.country: China (a Project 211 university in the southern part of China)
participants.quote: In total, 80 postgraduate students pursuing PhD degrees participated in this study.
participants.locator: pp. 7-8, Methodology, Participants (recruitment and assignment); p. 13, Data analysis (ANCOVA model); p. 19, Table 6 (survey); p. 20, Table 7 (reported proposal counts and inconsistent statistics)

ai_tool.name_model: Dou Bao (ByteDance), a chatbot built on large language models; model version not stated
ai_tool.how_used: Students held five weekly 30-minute individual dialogues with Dou Bao, typed or spoken, raising questions and receiving responses on the research perspective, research questions, literature, design and methods, and originality. The dialogues were audio-recorded and transcribed. The new proposal was written 'based on the discussions undertaken with either Dou Bao or a peer' (p. 10).

task.description: Create an innovative and practical research proposal, the paper's creative problem-solving (CPS) task.
task.duration: Three months, September through December (p. 8): a 3-hour training session, five weekly 30-minute dialogue sessions, a perception survey at the end of the experiment, then submission of a new proposal. The time spent writing the final proposal is not stated.

outcomes.name: Practical performance in CPS: research-proposal total score (stated maximum 100; minimum not stated)
outcomes.measure_detail: Composite rubric score of the submitted research proposal (p. 12, Measures of students' practical competencies in CPS; Appendix, Table 10, p. 26). Five dimensions have a maximum of 20 points each, with four scoring levels (20, 15, 10, 5): research objectives; research questions and hypotheses; literature review; research design and methods; and originality of the research. Originality is a full dimension and also appears in the research-questions descriptors; the remaining descriptors address clarity, significance, comprehensiveness, currency, and appropriateness. Only the total score is reported. The stated total maximum is 100; a total minimum is not stated and is not inferred from the rubric. Table 10 awards 5 even for absent proposal components. Proposals were anonymised and evaluated by two independent markers who received the criteria and model proposals; Kappa = 0.83 (p. 12). Human scoring is established, but neither expert nor lay/crowd-rater status is stated, so measure is null. The paper says the overall grade 'was calculated as the average score of each marking criteria score' (p. 12); the aggregation across criteria and markers is unclear and is not reconstructed. The ANCOVA covariate was each student's PhD-application proposal score, marked using the same rubric (pp. 9, 13); pretest descriptive statistics are not reported.
outcomes.delay: End-of-experiment post-test (p. 8, Figure 1; pp. 9-10, Procedure steps 4-5); the interval from the dialogue sessions to final proposal writing or submission is not stated.

contrasts.reported: Table 7: Experimental group N 40, Mean 57.77, SD 11.79, df 1, F 15.058***, Partial η2 0.179; Control group N 40, Mean 46.38, SD 12.85; ***p < 0.001. Text (p. 20): F = 15.058, p < 0.001; 'Partial η² = 0.17'; Levene's test F = 0.337, p = 0.568; homogeneity of regression slopes F = 1.734, p = 0.192. ANCOVA with the pretest proposal score as covariate (p. 13). Table 7 does not say whether the means are raw or covariate-adjusted, and pretest means are not reported. The N entries are printed counts, not independently verified complete-case ANCOVA counts: the table's F, numerator df, and partial eta-squared do not agree with 80 analyzed people under the stated model. No denominator df or explanation is given. The exact analyzed total and arm counts remain unresolved; the conditional consistency calculation in final.challenge_resolution is not substituted for the printed counts.
contrasts.locator: p. 20, RQ3 text and Table 7; p. 13, Data analysis (ANCOVA specification)

company_involvement.description: The AI tool, Dou Bao, is a ByteDance product, but the paper states no company role in the study. Funding: National Natural Science Foundation of China (62377014). The authors declare no conflict of interest.
company_involvement.locator: p. 9, Procedure step (3); p. 27, Funding and Competing interests

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1: the Methods explicitly state that the students were randomly assigned individually, 40 per arm, to Dou Bao or peer dialogue for developing an innovative research proposal; the control arm had no access to similar AI tools (pp. 8-9). The contradictory quasi-experimental label and absent allocation procedure remain an author-clarification item, but no nonrandom allocation mechanism is reported. Criterion 2: Table 7 reports 40 analyzed people per arm, exceeding 50 across arms (p. 20). Its ANCOVA statistics conflict with that exact count under the model on p. 13; the conditional alternative described in final.challenge_resolution also exceeds 50, so the threshold is met while exact analysis counts remain null. Criterion 3: two independent markers scored participants' submitted, anonymised proposals using a rubric that includes originality (pp. 10, 12, 26). The score is a mixed proposal-quality/originality composite, coded other. Unknown rater qualifications do not negate output scoring. AI was used for proposal development, but its availability during final writing or its removal before writing is not stated, so question and ai_available_when_produced are null; this prevents assigning with_ai versus after_ai, not the three-criterion eligibility decision.

one_line_finding: Dou Bao-assisted proposal development had higher reported composite proposal scores than peer dialogue (57.77, SD 11.79 vs 46.38, SD 12.85; Table 7 reports N = 40 per arm, ANCOVA F = 15.058, p < 0.001, partial η² = 0.179, but the exact analyzed sample is unresolved; p. 20).
open_questions: Composite construct and pooling: the scored rubric includes originality alongside proposal-quality criteria (p. 12; Table 10, p. 26), so criterion 3 is met and other remains the construct; whether to pool such composites is an Atlas analysis decision requiring no new source.
Dimension scores: originality and the other rubric dimensions have no separately reported results (pp. 12, 20, 26); authors would need to provide the dimension-level scores or summaries.

AI availability during final writing: step 5 requires a new proposal based on the prior dialogues but states neither continuing AI access nor AI removal (pp. 8-10, Figure 1 and Procedure). Both ai_available_when_produced and question are null; authors must clarify the final-writing instructions to distinguish with_ai from after_ai.

Assignment: the Methods say students were randomly assigned (p. 8), but the abstract, introduction, and procedure call the design quasi-experimental (pp. 1, 3, 8). No allocation procedure is described. Authors could confirm the allocation mechanism; a nonrandom mechanism would change criterion 1.

Control peers and independence: each control student chose one peer (p. 9), whose identity and membership in the study are not stated. Authors could clarify participant-pair links and possible dependence. Control access to similar AI tools was explicitly restricted (p. 8); the current concern is the appropriate uncertainty estimate, not failure of an eligibility criterion.

Table 7 means and baseline statistics: means are not labeled raw or adjusted, and pretest means and SDs are not reported (pp. 9, 13, 20). Authors could supply the ANCOVA output and baseline descriptive statistics.

Scoring aggregation and minimum: the paper states a maximum total of 100 and level scores 20, 15, 10, and 5, but describes the total as the average of marking-criterion scores (p. 12; Table 10, p. 26). The aggregation across dimensions and markers and the total minimum require author clarification; neither a zero minimum nor a derived minimum is recorded.

Marker qualifications: two independent markers received the criteria and model proposals, but their qualifications or professional roles are not identified (p. 12). measure is null pending authors' clarification of expert versus lay/crowd-rater status; human scoring itself is confirmed.

Design class field_rct versus lab_rct: students developed their own PhD research proposals during their first semester, but researchers arranged and recorded the sessions (pp. 8-10). field_rct is retained provisionally; authors could confirm whether the task was ordinary degree work or a separate research exercise. Either randomized design class is core.

Exact ANCOVA sample: Table 7 reports N = 40 per arm, while its F, numerator df, and partial eta-squared conflict with that total under the stated ANCOVA model (pp. 13, 20). Exact analyzed total and arm counts are null. Authors must provide the complete-case counts, denominator df, missing-case accounting, and corrected ANCOVA output. The reported and conditionally implied totals both exceed the eligibility threshold.

Survey sample discrepancy: Table 6 analyzed 36 students per arm, whereas 40 per arm were randomized (pp. 8, 19); the paper gives no reason for the difference. Authors could explain the missing survey responses, but this self-report outcome does not establish the qualifying proposal sample.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are not scored on the creative output: RQ1 dialogue-move percentages coded from 80 transcripts (Tables 2-3, p. 14; the speculation category, which the authors read as exploring novel ideas, did not differ: 17.08 vs 16.14 percent, t = 0.928, p = 0.356, Table 2) and lag-sequential residuals (Tables 4-5, pp. 16-17; Figs. 2-3, p. 18); RQ2 self-reported perceptions (perceived usefulness, ease of use, intention to use; Table 6, p. 19, N = 36 per group). Interviews with 18 randomly selected experimental-group students are qualitative (pp. 10, 19-20). Data are 'available upon reasonable request' (p. 27); there is no data or code URL. The authors call the sample small and the duration short (p. 23). The search record says the paper is CP08 in Holzner et al. 2025; that fact comes from candidates.json, not from this document. Reconciliation: B's text in the delay and data_url fields was moved to open_questions and notes, where A had recorded the same facts. Finalization: the full markdown conversion, including the Appendix and references, was read; eligibility passages and retained statistics were checked in the PDF. Figure 1 and the image-only publication date on p. 27 were inspected directly. No additional qualifying output outcome was found. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the historical reconciliation; its statements about verified analysis counts, provisional expert status, and final-writing AI availability are superseded by the current fields and final object. No unresolved reconciliation differences were present. The source does not settle the exact ANCOVA sample; conditional arithmetic is retained only as an inconsistency check, not as an observed count or an extracted effect size.

differences.resolved: other, as in B. The outcome is the sum of five 20-point rubric dimensions. Originality of the research is one dimension, and originality also appears in the level descriptors of the research-questions dimension. The other criteria rate the clarity, significance, comprehensiveness, currency, and appropriateness of the proposal. The paper calls the total practical performance in CPS, and no marker judges creativity as a whole, so overall_creativity ('a rating or score of creativity as a whole') does not fit. The originality component rules out usefulness. The reconciled c114 and c154 code 100-point sums of mixed rubric dimensions as other (c101 coded a composite as usefulness because that paper called it design quality). measure_detail describes the rubric, and open_questions asks Review 1 whether such composites join the with_ai pool.
differences.quote: and finally, producing innovative contributions, which leads to originality of research. The marking criteria included 5 dimensions. The full score for each dimension was 20, meaning the highest possible total score was 100.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1 participants.n_analyzed and arms[*].n_analyzed were treated as verified despite incompatible Table 7 ANCOVA statistics.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: The source confirms the printed N = 40 in each arm, but cannot settle the actual ANCOVA sample or identify which printed statistic is wrong. Set the exact analyzed total and arm counts to null, retained every printed Table 7 value in reported, and added the inconsistency to exclusions, eligibility, the finding, and open_questions. Independently checked the conditional identity df_error = F * df_effect * (1 - partial eta-squared) / partial eta-squared: F = 15.058, df_effect = 1, and partial eta-squared = 0.179 imply approximately 69 error degrees of freedom; rounding permits only that integer. For the stated two-group ANCOVA with one covariate, this conditionally corresponds to 72 people, whereas 80 would give 77 error degrees of freedom. These are diagnostic calculations, not reported counts, and neither 72 nor any inferred arm allocation replaces the source. Table 6's 36 per arm belongs to the perception survey and does not establish the proposal-analysis sample. Authors must resolve the inconsistency; both the reported and conditional totals exceed 50, so criterion 2 remains met.

open_items.item: Composite rubric eligibility and pooling: originality is scored on the submitted proposal, so criterion 3 is met; pooling mixed composites is an Atlas analysis decision (p. 12; Table 10, p. 26).
Unreported originality and other rubric-dimension scores: authors could provide separate scores or summaries; these affect construct-specific extraction, not criterion 3 (pp. 12, 20, 26).

AI access during final proposal writing or explicit removal: authors could supply final-writing instructions; this settles with_ai versus after_ai, while assigned AI assistance and output scoring are already established (pp. 8-10).

Random assignment versus the quasi-experimental label: authors could provide the actual allocation procedure. Criterion 1 is currently met by the explicit Methods statement; evidence of a nonrandom mechanism would change eligibility (pp. 1, 3, 8).
Control-peer identities and participant-pair dependence: authors could provide the pairing structure and peer membership; this determines appropriate uncertainty estimates (pp. 8-9).
Raw versus adjusted Table 7 means and absent pretest means/SDs: authors could provide the analysis output and baseline summaries (pp. 9, 13, 20).

Aggregation across rubric criteria and markers, and total score minimum: authors could specify the scoring algorithm; the stated maximum and direct originality scoring already establish an eligible output measure (pp. 12, 26).
Marker qualifications: authors could identify their professional roles or expertise to settle the measure subtype; two independent human markers are already confirmed (p. 12).
field_rct versus lab_rct: authors could confirm whether proposal development formed ordinary degree work or a separate study exercise; either randomized class is core (pp. 8-10).

Exact ANCOVA total and arm counts, missing cases, denominator df, and inconsistent F/partial eta-squared: authors must supply corrected analysis output. This does not change the 50-person threshold on the available reported and conditional counts (pp. 13, 20); exact counts remain null.

Unexplained perception-survey sample shortfall: authors could account for the 36 analyzed per arm versus 40 assigned per arm; survey completeness does not decide proposal-outcome eligibility (pp. 8, 19).
